interviewQuestions.question: YOLO vs Faster R-CNN — which do you pick for a real-time app?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the actual trade-off: Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector — it proposes candidate regions first, then classifies and refines each one — which generally gives higher accuracy, especially on small or overlapping objects, but at real cost in speed, typically running well under 15 fps. YOLO is one-stage — a single network pass predicts all boxes and classes at once — which is what makes it capable of real-time throughput, often 30+ fps or higher depending on the variant and hardware. For a real-time app — say, a live camera feature or an autonomous-driving perception module — I'd pick YOLO, because meeting the latency budget is a hard constraint the product cannot function without, whereas the accuracy gap versus Faster R-CNN has narrowed substantially in recent YOLO versions and is often an acceptable trade for staying real-time. I'd only reconsider this if the specific objects being detected are very small relative to the frame (where two-stage detectors historically hold a bigger edge) or if the app can tolerate offline/batch processing instead of live inference.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the actual speed/accuracy trade-off with correct reasoning, rather than just naming YOLO as the default answer without justification.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: One-stage vs two-stage for a latency-critical product

interviewQuestions.question: What problem do anchor boxes solve, and why not just have the network predict box coordinates directly?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Predicting a bounding box from nothing means the network has to output four raw numbers (x, y, width, height) across an enormous possible range, for objects that could be anywhere in the image at any scale — that's a much harder regression problem than it sounds, especially early in training when the network has no prior at all about where objects tend to be. Anchor boxes solve this by giving the network a strong starting guess: tile the image with a dense grid of predefined boxes at various sizes and aspect ratios, and instead of predicting a box from scratch, the network only has to predict two much easier things per anchor — does this anchor contain an object, and what small offset adjusts this anchor's coordinates to better fit it.

That reframing matters because it turns an unconstrained regression problem into a much better-conditioned one: the anchor already encodes a reasonable prior for typical object shapes (a wide anchor for cars, a tall one for pedestrians, chosen ahead of time based on the dataset's actual object statistics), so the network learns small corrections rather than absolute positions.

The trade-off is that anchor choice becomes a real design decision — anchors mismatched to your actual object shapes (e.g. reusing car-shaped anchors for a dataset of tall, narrow objects) hurt performance for reasons that look like a modeling failure but are actually a configuration failure.

**Testing:** whether you understand anchors as reframing a hard regression problem into an easier offset-prediction one, not just as a mechanical implementation detail.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why anchor boxes exist

interviewQuestions.question: Your detector reports high mAP on the validation set but users complain it misses small, distant objects in real footage. How do you dig into that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
mAP is averaged across all classes and often across a range of IoU thresholds, so a genuine weakness on one object-size bucket can be almost invisible in the headline number if large/medium objects dominate the dataset and are detected well. My first move is to stop trusting the aggregate and slice the metric: compute AP separately for small, medium, and large objects (by pixel area, following the standard COCO-style size buckets), and separately per class if small objects cluster in a few classes. That slicing alone usually confirms or kills the hypothesis quickly.

If small objects are genuinely the weak spot, the causes are fairly specific and worth checking in order: whether the anchor sizes actually cover the small-object scale present in real footage (anchors tuned for the validation set's typical object size can simply miss much smaller real-world instances); whether the backbone's downsampling has already destroyed small objects' spatial signal by the layer detection happens on — this is exactly why architectures use multi-scale feature maps (feature pyramids) specifically so small objects get detected from higher-resolution, less-downsampled features rather than only the deepest layer; and whether NMS's IoU threshold is too aggressive and suppressing legitimately separate small, closely-packed objects as duplicates.

I'd also sanity-check that the validation set's object-size distribution actually matches real footage — a mismatch there would explain a good validation mAP that doesn't predict real-world small-object performance at all.

**Testing:** whether you know to slice a misleading aggregate metric by object size before proposing architectural fixes, and can name the concrete small-object failure modes (anchor scale, downsampling loss, NMS threshold).
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging small-object detection failures
